# Languages

Field's small languages, from the host side. A box can be *written* in one of them — a per-box property picks the language and a `BoxExecution` runs it, which is how `datalog`, `forth`, `nano`, `morpho`, `clojure`, `python`, FieldML and the two `remotejs` runtimes work — or a program can be *embedded*, a triple-quoted Kotlin string whose first line names the language and whose contents are compiled on the JVM, which is how RectSL and StackSL work. What is documented below is the Kotlin that either shape hands you: the compiler you give a program to, the result and the diagnostics it gives back, and the bridge a running program calls host values through. The notation itself is on the cheatsheets, and that is where the pictures are. Read `Datalog.kt` first — it is the smallest complete example of the shape all of these have, a value you add source to, query, and then ask `why` of — then `DatalogEngine.kt` for what the implementation underneath actually costs, `StackSL.kt` for the compile-and-diagnose surface both embedded languages share, `ForthInterpreter.kt` and `NanoVM.kt` for the two implementations you can read end to end in a sitting, and `HostBridge.kt` for FieldML's reflective JVM bridge — the file to read before wiring any language to Kotlin values. `dev_docs/` carries the map of what a new language has to touch on the way in, in `small_language_anatomy.md`, which is also the guarded list of which languages exist. The prose, with pictures: [Language extensions](../language_extensions.md) for the route decision, then [Datalog](../datalog.md), [RectSL](../rectsl_cheatsheet.md), [StackSL](../stacksl_cheatsheet.md), [FieldML](../fieldml_cheatsheet.md), [MorphoHDL](../morpho_examples.md), [Nano](../nano_examples.md), [Forth](../forth_examples.md) and [Python](../python.md).

## ClojureInterface.kt { #clojureinterface-kt }

Clojure as a Field main language: a box whose source is Clojure, evaluated by the real Clojure
runtime on this JVM.

Nothing here implements a Lisp. `clojure.jar` is on the classpath and this file is the adapter
between Field's box-execution contract and `clojure.java.api.Clojure` — which is why the whole
language is one file while `afield.datalog` and `afield.rectsl`, whose compilers Field owns, are
packages.

Read it in four layers:

 - [`ClojureHost`](languages.md#clojureinterface-kt-clojurehost) is the interpreter, and the only part with no Field in it. It reads one top-level
   form at a time and evaluates it, which is `load-string`'s own loop written out so that the
   *line* each form started on is available while that form runs: that line is what lets printed
   output land beside the form that printed it, the way it does in every other kind of Field box.
   It returns the value of the last form, and `executeIfFn` will invoke that value when it is an
   `IFn` — a host convenience, off on the box path ([`ClojureExecution`](languages.md#clojureinterface-kt-clojureexecution) passes `false`), so a box
   whose last form evaluates to a function prints the function rather than calling it.
   `compileOnly` is the same read loop with evaluation withheld, which is where the editor's
   syntax errors come from, carrying line and column.
 - [`ClojureInterface`](languages.md#clojureinterface-kt-clojureinterface) is the host facade: the box currently running, and the handful of Field
   verbs that are awkward to reach by raw interop because they are Kotlin extension functions
   with default arguments. `field/core.clj` (in `src/jvmMain/resources`) is the Clojure side of
   it, `require`d and `refer`red into every box namespace, so a box can say `(lines ls :fit true)`
   rather than naming `SomeSkikoKt`.
 - [`ClojureExecution`](languages.md#clojureinterface-kt-clojureexecution) is the `BoxExecution`, so it is the half that knows about boxes: output
   proxying, `is-running`, per-fragment generation counting, and `complete`, whose candidates
   come from Compliment if that namespace loads and from nothing if it does not — completion is
   optional here by design rather than by omission.
 - `installClojure` and `clojureTopologyNeedsUpdating` are the registration, and they are
   identical in shape to every other main language: one `registerMainLanguageRuntime` call, one
   `TopologyWatcher` that swaps a child box's execution when the graph changes.

One namespace, not one per box: every Clojure box in every open document evaluates in `live.user`
(Clojure namespaces are per-JVM, and [`ClojureExecution`](languages.md#clojureinterface-kt-clojureexecution) asks for that one name), so two Clojure
boxes are two cells of one notebook. `public/docs/clojure.md` is the page that says so to a
reader; `dev_docs/small_language_anatomy.md` is the map of the integration points.

## Datalog.kt { #datalog-kt }

The facade over parser and engine: a [`Datalog`](languages.md#datalog-kt-datalog) holds a program, answers queries as [`DlRows`](languages.md#datalog-kt-dlrows), and
reconstructs the proof of a derived fact.

Nothing here parses or evaluates. [`DatalogParser`](languages.md#datalogparser-kt-datalogparser) turns text into the [`DlUnit`](languages.md#datalogast-kt-dlunit) this file merges
and [`DatalogEngine`](languages.md#datalogengine-kt-datalogengine) computes the model; what is left is the part a caller touches — holding the
program, noticing when the cached model has gone stale, and sorting rows so that a query prints
the same way twice, which set semantics on their own do not promise.

The exception is the top-down proof search behind `why`, which is here rather than in the engine
because it reads a finished model instead of building one. It walks rules backwards from a
derived fact, bounded by the round numbers the fixpoint recorded, and picks premises in the same
order the planner would. The opposite question, why a goal has no answers at all, is
`DatalogWhyNot.kt`.

`import afield.datalog.*` is in every Kotlin box's preamble, so `Datalog()` and the `Dl` types
are in scope with nothing to import.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/datalog/Datalog.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/datalog/Datalog/)

## DatalogAst.kt { #datalogast-kt }

The abstract syntax of Field's Datalog — see [`Datalog`](languages.md#datalog-kt-datalog) for the facade, [`DatalogParser`](languages.md#datalogparser-kt-datalogparser) for the
concrete syntax and [`DatalogEngine`](languages.md#datalogengine-kt-datalogengine) for what evaluates this.

Everything here is a value type with structural equality, because the engine leans on that in two
places: rules are de-duplicated when the same text is executed twice (a live box re-runs its whole
program on every keystroke-triggered execute), and derived rows are stored in hash sets.

Names are `Dl`-prefixed. Boxes get `import afield.datalog.*` for free (see
`afield.intro`), on top of `afield.*` and `afield.stdlib.*`, so an unprefixed `Var`, `Atom` or
`Rule` in this package would be a name collision waiting to happen in user code.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/datalog/DatalogAst.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/datalog/DatalogAst/)

## DatalogBoxes.kt { #datalogboxes-kt }

The Field bridge: the live box graph as Datalog base relations.

This is the reason for having a Datalog in here rather than shelling out to one. A Field document
*is* a labelled graph — boxes, parent/child edges, nesting, and a property bag per box — and the
questions you actually ask of it while working ("which boxes does nothing run into?", "which two
boxes both bind the same property?", "what is downstream of this one?") are recursive joins,
which is precisely what `afield.graphquery`'s path language cannot express and this can.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val d = Datalog()
d.addBoxGraph(thisBox)
d.add("""
    reaches(A, B) :- child(A, B).
    reaches(A, C) :- reaches(A, B), child(B, C).
    orphan(X) :- box(X), !child(_, X).
""")
println(d.query("orphan(X), name(X, N)").table())
```

## DatalogEngine.kt { #datalogengine-kt }

Storage and evaluation: indexed relations, a safety-directed body planner, stratification, and a
semi-naive fixpoint.

Three invariants hold the thing together, and each one buys a feature:

 - **Rows are planned, not interpreted.** Each rule is compiled once into a list of `DlStep`s over
   integer variable slots, and the planner decides statically whether each argument position binds
   or filters. Nothing consults a "is this variable bound yet" map at join time.
 - **Facts derived in a round are not visible until the round ends.** New rows go to a pending
   buffer and are merged at the end of the iteration, so every fact's `DlRelation.roundOf` is
   strictly greater than the rounds of the facts that derived it. That is what makes
   `Datalog.why` terminate without an occurs-check hack: a proof may only descend to
   strictly earlier rounds. The counter is *global*, not per-stratum, so the same ordering holds
   across a stratum boundary and a proof may descend through negation and aggregation too.
 - **Negation and aggregation are stratified.** Both are "negative" edges in the dependency graph;
   a negative edge inside a strongly-connected component is rejected up front with the cycle
   spelled out, rather than producing an answer that depends on evaluation order.

## DatalogInterface.kt { #dataloginterface-kt }

Datalog as a box language: the [`DatalogExecution`](languages.md#dataloginterface-kt-datalogexecution) that runs fragments inside a box, and the
registration that puts Datalog in the Main Language menu.

[`DatalogExecution`](languages.md#dataloginterface-kt-datalogexecution) is the `BoxExecution`. It merges a fragment into the box's accumulated
program, prints whatever that fragment asked for, and completes on the relations the box has
actually defined as well as on the builtin functions, the aggregate operators and the box-graph
names. `installDatalog` registers the runtime and the persistent `isDatalogRoot` flag, and
`datalogTopologyNeedsUpdating` attaches and detaches executions as boxes are marked and unmarked.

The `#directives` are the Field-specific part, and the reason this is more than a thin adapter:
`#boxes` loads the live document into the base relations of `dlBoxRelationSchema`, `#why` and
`#whynot` reach the two provenance layers, and `#program` prints back what the box has
accumulated. `directiveHelp` is the one list that `#help` prints and completion offers, so a
directive added to it appears in both.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/datalog/DatalogInterface.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/datalog/DatalogInterface/)

## DatalogObjects.kt { #datalogobjects-kt }

Any live object graph as Datalog base relations, by way of `afield.graphquery`.

The two layers answer different halves of the same question. `graphPaths` addresses slots by
pattern and hands back live lenses, but a glob cannot follow an edge and then follow it again, and
it has nothing to say about two addresses that turn out to be the same object. Datalog has
recursion, negation and aggregation and no idea what an object is. Joining them costs one walk:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val d = Datalog()
d.addObjectGraph(rig)
d.add(dlObjectGraphRules)
d.query("alias(A, B)")                                  // two names for one object
d.query("reaches(\"carrier\", P), writable(P)")         // settable, anywhere below carrier
```

Identity is what makes it worth the trip. `dlObjectGraphSchema`'s `at(Path, ObjectId)` gives every
non-scalar value a number, so aliasing needs no special relation — it is a join of `at` with
itself. The walk already visits a shared node under every alias (its cycle detection is
path-scoped, not visit-once), so the facts are there to be joined.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/datalog/DatalogObjects.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/datalog/DatalogObjects/)

## DatalogParser.kt { #datalogparser-kt }

Source text to abstract syntax: the lexer and recursive-descent parser every Datalog program in
Field goes through, and the two word lists that decide what the notation reserves.

There is no error recovery. The first thing the parser cannot read raises a [`DlException`](languages.md#datalogast-kt-dlexception)
carrying the line and column it stopped at, and the box language turns those into an error marker
on the offending line, so a program is either whole or it is a single message.

Two of the tables outlive the parse. `DatalogParser.functions` and `DatalogParser.aggregateOps`
are what the box language offers in its completion popup, and the browser-side highlighter keeps
its own copy of both; `afield.examples.datalog.DatalogEditorExtensionWorkout` runs the shipped
JavaScript against these sets and fails when the two have drifted apart.

## DatalogWhyNot.kt { #datalogwhynot-kt }

The why-not layer: `Datalog.whyNot` walks a failing conjunction literal by literal and names the
one that took the answer count to zero.

`Datalog.why` accounts for a fact that is present. This accounts for a query that is empty, which
is the commoner question and the one a saturated model cannot be asked directly. [`DlWhyNot`](languages.md#datalogwhynot-kt-dlwhynot) is
the result, [`DlNarrowing`](languages.md#datalogwhynot-kt-dlnarrowing) one step of the walk, and `#whynot <goal>` in a Datalog box is the way
in.

Everything here is written against the public [`Datalog`](languages.md#datalog-kt-datalog) surface, which is why it is a file of its
own rather than more of the fixpoint's. The counts it reports are the engine's rather than a
second implementation's: each prefix of the conjunction is synthesised into a rule and put
through [`DatalogEngine`](languages.md#datalogengine-kt-datalogengine), at a cost of one solve per literal.

## ForthInterpreter.kt { #forthinterpreter-kt }

ForthField — a compact, extensible Forth used by Field4 for live coding.

It is host-driven:
- it executes ForthField source and keeps its own data stack/dictionary
- it ships with creative-coding oriented builtins (vectors + `FLine`)
- it can be extended at runtime from Kotlin via `defineWord`
- it can interoperate with host objects using `@?` / `@?!` reflection calls

### The host loop

Typical host loop:
1. Construct an interpreter once (`val forth = ForthInterpreter()`).
2. Register host bridge words with `defineWord` as needed.
3. Push host objects (buffers, context values, services) onto `stack`.
4. Run `eval(...)`.
5. Pop resulting values (for example an `FLine`) and hand them to rendering/output code.

Example: basic execution and stack access:
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val forth = ForthInterpreter()
val diagnostics = forth.eval("2 3 +")
check(diagnostics.isEmpty())
println(forth.popNum()) // 5.0
```

Example: defining words in ForthField:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
: sqr ( n -- n2 ) dup * ;
: hypot2 ( x y -- d2 ) sqr swap sqr + ;
3 4 hypot2 .
```

Example: create an `FLine` shape in ForthField:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
: stroke-ribbon ( -- f )
  fline
  0   0   moveto
  120 20  lineto
  160 90  210 90  260 20 cubicto
  320 0   lineto
  true  fline-stroked
  false fline-filled
  1.0 0.55 0.2 1.0 fline-color
  2.5 fline-thickness ;

stroke-ribbon
```

Host-side consumption of the resulting `FLine`:
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val forth = ForthInterpreter()
val source = """
  : stroke-ribbon ( -- f )
    fline
    0 0 moveto
    120 20 lineto
    160 90 210 90 260 20 cubicto
    true fline-stroked
    1 0.55 0.2 1 fline-color
    2.5 fline-thickness ;
  stroke-ribbon
""".trimIndent()

val diagnostics = forth.eval(source)
if (diagnostics.isEmpty()) {
  val line = forth.pop() as FLine
  // Forward `line` into your output channel / renderer.
}
```

Example: use vector helpers with FLine convenience words:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
: zig ( -- f )
  fline
  0   0   vec2 fline-moveto-v2
  40  20  vec2 fline-lineto-v2
  80 -10  vec2 fline-lineto-v2
  120 25  vec2 fline-lineto-v2
  1 0 0 1 fline-node-color ;
zig
```

### The reflection bridge

Example: resolve classes without full FQNs.
`class-for` consults Field's class cache (`importHelp.kt`) so short names usually work.

```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
s"FLine" class-for @? getName println
s"Vec3"  class-for @? getName println

s"Fli" class-matches print   \ returns a list of FQNs
s"Fli" class-help            \ prints one-per-line suggestions
```

Example: reflection bridge (`@?` / `@?!`) with `FLine`, built entirely by class lookup.
This demonstrates construction + method calls without using the `fline` helper.

```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
variable f
s"FLine" class-for @? newInstance f !

\ Explicit arity call: f.moveTo(Number, Number, Number)
f @ 0   0   0   3 @?! moveTo drop

\ Explicit arity call: f.lineTo(Number, Number, Number)
f @ 120 30  0   3 @?! lineTo drop
f @ 220 10  0   3 @?! lineTo drop
f @ 260 80 0  320 80 0  380 20 0  9 @?! cubicTo drop

\ Properties are just a map on FLine
f @ @? properties  s"thickness" 2.5 2 @?! put
f @ @? properties  s"stroked" true 2 @?! put

\ Heuristic call for zero-arg methods works well with @?
f @ @? close drop

\ Leave the final FLine on the stack
f @
```

Example: `@?` reads data too (field/getter/method fallback):
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
f @ @? nodes   \ push internal node list
@? size .      \ call size() on that list and print node count
```

Example: constructor with explicit args via `@?! new`:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
variable sb
s"StringBuilder" class-for s"hello" 1 @?! new sb !
sb @ @? toString println
```

Example: extending ForthField with Kotlin bridge words.
Here we expose a helper that appends a `vec4` worth of floats into any
`DynamicallyWriteable` buffer (for example `VulkanBuffer` or `FrameBufferGroup`).

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
import afield.four.buffers.DynamicallyWriteable
import afield.stdlib.Vec4

val forth = ForthInterpreter()
forth.defineWord("append-vec4", "( buf x y z w -- buf )") {
  val w = popNum().toFloat()
  val z = popNum().toFloat()
  val y = popNum().toFloat()
  val x = popNum().toFloat()
  val buf = pop() as DynamicallyWriteable

  buf.append {
    put(Vec4(x, y, z, w))
  }
  push(buf)
}
```

Example: call that bridge word from ForthField after pushing a host buffer:
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
forth.push(myDynamicBuffer) // host object: VulkanBuffer / FrameBufferGroup / similar
forth.eval("""
  0.0 1.0 0.0 1.0 append-vec4
  1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 append-vec4
  0.0 0.0 1.0 1.0 append-vec4
""".trimIndent())
```

Example: long-form output areas from ForthField:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
s"<b>Inline-ish output area content</b>" html
s"<pre>Detailed log text...</pre>" s"debug" html-channel
```

Example: launchable animation with cooperative yielding via `frame`.
Run this in Launch mode (or call `begin("default")` on the box), so `spinner` executes
every RunLoop tick. `frame` yields immediately, letting the rest of Field proceed.
Store evolving state in variables, because each strand tick re-enters the word from the top.

```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
variable tick
variable line
0 tick !

: spinner ( -- )
  s"FLine" class-for @? newInstance line !

  \ center point
  line @ 0 0 0 3 @?! moveTo drop

  \ animated endpoint (simple circular motion)
  line @
  tick @ 0.05 * dup cos 120 *          ( x )
             swap sin 120 *            ( x y )
  0 3 @?! lineTo drop

  \ style via reflected property map
  line @ @? properties s"thickness" 2.0 2 @?! put
  line @ @? properties s"stroked" true 2 @?! put
  line @ s"geom" display-channel

  \ show a debug line in output area
  s"tick=" tick @ str str+ s"debug" display-channel

  1 tick +!
  frame
;

spinner
```

Example: same pattern with an explicit ForthField loop.
`frame` exits the current tick immediately; on next tick the word starts again.

```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
variable phase
0 phase !

: pulse-loop ( -- )
  begin
    s"phase=" phase @ str str+ println
    1 phase +!
    frame
  again ;

pulse-loop
```

Example: full overwrite of float data each tick, since `write` replaces the payload rather than
adding to it:
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
import afield.four.buffers.DynamicallyWriteable

forth.defineWord("write-triangle", "( buf -- buf )") {
  val buf = pop() as DynamicallyWriteable
  buf.write {
    // XYZW packed per vertex (3 vertices)
    put(-0.5f); put(-0.5f); put(0f); put(1f)
    put( 0.5f); put(-0.5f); put(0f); put(1f)
    put( 0.0f); put( 0.5f); put(0f); put(1f)
  }
  push(buf)
}
```

Notes for dynamic-buffer bridging:
- `defineWord` closures execute on the interpreter thread/context used by your host.
- Prefer `write { ... }` when replacing the payload; `append { ... }` when accumulating.
- `DynamicBuffer.put(Vec4)` follows std430-friendly alignment rules used by Field's buffer code.
- If you need explicit control, call `putScalar(...)` repeatedly instead of vector helpers.

### Builtins

Builtins included by default:
- stack ops (`dup`, `swap`, `over`, `pick`, `roll`, ...)
- math/logic/control flow (`if/else/then`, `begin/until`, `do/loop`, ...)
- variables/constants (`variable`, `!`, `@`, `constant`)
- strings/output (`."..."`, `s"..."`, `.`, `println`, ...)
- dictionary tools (`words`, `see`, `forget`, `recurse`)
- return-stack transfer (`>r`, `r>`, `r@`)
- vectors (`vec2`, `vec3`, `vec4` + arithmetic helpers)
- `FLine` primitives (`fline`, `moveto`, `lineto`, `cubicto`, styling words)
- small visualization words (`html`, `watch`, `stack-display`, `bar`, `plot-stack`)
- frame/yield primitive (`frame`) for cooperative launch-mode animations
- host reflection hooks (`@?`, `@?!`, `class-for`, `class-matches`, `class-help`)

### Dictionary, recursion and the return stack

Dictionary / debugging examples:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
: sqr dup * ;
words              \ print all currently known words
see sqr            \ print ": sqr dup * ;"
forget sqr         \ remove the user-defined word
```

Recursion example:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
: countdown ( n -- )
  dup 0> if
    dup println
    1- recurse
  else
    drop
  then ;
5 countdown
```

Infinite loop example. Use `again` mainly in launched words where `frame`
yields back to Field each tick:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
variable tick
: ticker begin tick @ println 1 tick +! frame again ;
ticker
```

Return-stack examples. `>r` moves a temporary value away from the data stack,
`r@` copies it back, and `r>` restores/removes it:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
: add-twice ( a b -- a+b+b )
  >r        \ return stack: b ; data stack: a
  r@ +      \ data stack: a+b, b is still saved
  r> + ;    \ data stack: a+b+b
```

### Visualization words

Visualization examples:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
s"<b>Hello from Forth</b>" html
0.72 1.0 s"progress" bar
42 s"answer" watch
stack-display
1 4 9 16 plot-stack
```

## Expr.kt { #expr-kt }

FieldML's surface syntax tree: one node per piece of written syntax, each carrying the source
range it was parsed from.

[`Parser`](languages.md#parser-kt-parser) produces this tree and [`Inferencer`](languages.md#inferencer-kt-inferencer) reads it. Nothing in it has a type yet. Every node
here has a counterpart in `afield.ml.type` that carries an inferred type, and that typed tree is
lowered again into the `afield.ml.core` form the evaluator runs.

The tree is narrower than the syntax in two places. [`ECall`](languages.md#expr-kt-ecall) takes a single argument, so
application is already curried when it is parsed: `add 20 22` is `ECall(ECall(add, 20), 22)`. The
pipe operator builds that same node with its left operand as the argument, so `10 |> add 5` and
`add 5 10` differ only in the ranges they record. And a constructor's argument types are bare
names: [`TypeRef`](languages.md#expr-kt-typeref) has one case, [`TypeRefName`](languages.md#expr-kt-typerefname), so a run of names in `type Tree a = Node Tree Tree`
reads as a run of separate arguments. Inference resolves each name to a built-in type, to the type
being declared, to one of that type's own parameters, or to a data type with no arguments.

It is wider than the syntax in one place: [`ELet`](languages.md#expr-kt-elet) and [`ELambda`](languages.md#expr-kt-elambda) keep the parameter list as it was
written, so `let add a b = ...` is one node with two parameters. Folding those into nested arrow
types is inference's job, and turning them into nested one-parameter lambdas is the lowering's.

[`ELet`](languages.md#expr-kt-elet) and [`ETypeDecl`](languages.md#expr-kt-etypedecl) both carry a `body`, and for a top-level binding that body is the whole
rest of the program: a box's bindings stack up by nesting inside each other. A `let` with nothing
after it gets `EVar("Unit")` for a body.

## Core.kt { #core-kt }

The tree FieldML actually evaluates: the typed tree with its source positions dropped and its
multi-parameter lambdas curried into one-parameter [`CLam`](languages.md#core-kt-clam) nodes.

[`Lowerer`](languages.md#lowerer-kt-lowerer) is the only thing that builds one and [`Evaluator`](languages.md#evaluator-kt-evaluator) the only thing that walks one. Every
case here corresponds to a case of the typed tree, and the lowering is a case-for-case mapping
apart from the lambda, so the two hierarchies are easy to read side by side.

What the lowering leaves behind is as informative as what it keeps. Types stay on every node, so a
later pass can still ask what a subexpression is. Ranges do not, so an evaluation failure carries
no position of its own, and a box reports it against the fragment that was run rather than the
subexpression that failed. [`CLet`](languages.md#core-kt-clet) keeps the `recursive` flag but has no parameter list, because by
this point a `let f x = ...`'s parameters are the lambda sitting in its `value`.
[`CoreConstructor`](languages.md#core-kt-coreconstructor) keeps a constructor's name and arity and drops its type scheme, which has
already done its work in inference.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ml/core/Core.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ml/core/Core/)

## HostTypes.kt { #hosttypes-kt }

The reflection behind FieldML's host types: what a [`THost`](languages.md#types-kt-thost) names, and what can therefore be said
at type-check time about a member's type, a resolved overload's result, the parameter slots a
call's arguments land in, and the members a receiver actually has.

A [`THost`](languages.md#types-kt-thost)'s name is a real JVM class name, which is what keeps a program typed once it reaches
into the JVM: a member access is inferred rather than left dynamic, a misspelled member name is
reported where it is written instead of crashing on the first run, and completion has a class to
enumerate.

Two rules bound what this file will claim.

*`Host` stays the dynamic type.* `OPAQUE`, the name `Host` itself, is what a host type degrades to
whenever reflection cannot justify anything better: a generic erased to `Object`, an array, a
`Map`, a nullable return, an overload set whose best candidates disagree about what they return.
`Inferencer.unifyHosts` lets it stand for any class, which is the statement "unknown, checked at
run time". It is a *bounded* dynamic type rather than a universal one, though:
`Inferencer.requireDynamicallyReachable` refuses a `Host` where a function, a list, a tuple or a
record is wanted, and names what to reach for instead.

*A mapping only claims what the runtime actually does.* `fieldMLTypeOf` answers with the type
`afield.ml.core.hostToFieldMLValue` will really produce, so reflection saying `int` means an
`IntValue` arrives, and `List<Double>` means a list of floats. Where the declared type does not
determine the converted one the answer is `Host` rather than something plausible: a `Map` really
does convert to a record, but its field names are nowhere in the declared type, so the type side
says `Host` and the program reads the fields with `hostGet`.

## TypedAst.kt { #typedast-kt }

FieldML's syntax tree after inference: the same shape as the surface tree in `afield.ml.ast`, with
a [`Type`](languages.md#types-kt-type) on every expression and on every pattern.

[`Inferencer`](languages.md#inferencer-kt-inferencer) produces it and [`Lowerer`](languages.md#lowerer-kt-lowerer) consumes it. Source ranges survive inference, which is what
lets a type error point at the text that caused it, and this is the last stage to have them: the
`afield.ml.core` tree the evaluator runs keeps the types and drops the positions.

Three things here are inference's findings rather than a restatement of the syntax:

  - `TExprLet.recursive` is true for the `let f x = ...` function form, which is the form whose
    own name is in scope inside its body.
  - `TExprLet.parameters` repeats the parameters of the lambda that the binding's value became,
    and is empty when the value is not a lambda.
  - [`TypedConstructor`](languages.md#typedast-kt-typedconstructor) gives each constructor of a declared data type its arity and the [`Scheme`](languages.md#types-kt-scheme)
    its name was bound under, so `Some` is an ordinary curried function from there on.

`walkTyped` is the one walker over the hierarchy, and completion is its caller: it compiles a
probe program and looks for the [`TExprLambda`](languages.md#typedast-kt-texprlambda) whose parameter names match the lambda under the
caret, which is how a callback's parameters have types before a reader has written any.

## Types.kt { #types-kt }

The types FieldML infers, and the two ways one is printed back to a reader.

[`Type`](languages.md#types-kt-type) is the vocabulary inference works in: five ground types, a unification variable [`TVar`](languages.md#types-kt-tvar), an
arrow [`TFun`](languages.md#types-kt-tfun), the structural cases [`TRecord`](languages.md#types-kt-trecord), [`TTuple`](languages.md#types-kt-ttuple) and [`TList`](languages.md#types-kt-tlist), [`TAdt`](languages.md#types-kt-tadt) for a declared data
type applied to its arguments, and [`THost`](languages.md#types-kt-thost) for a JVM type reached over the host bridge, whose
`name` is what `FieldMLHostTypes` reflects on. [`TFun`](languages.md#types-kt-tfun) takes one argument at a time, matching the
curried application the parser builds, so a function of two arguments is `TFun(a, TFun(b, c))`.

A [`Scheme`](languages.md#types-kt-scheme) is a type together with the variable ids generalised over it, and it can restrict what
those ids are allowed to become. An id listed in `numeric` only unifies with `Int` or `Float`, and
one listed in `vector` only with `Vec2`, `Vec3` or `Vec4`. That is how the prelude gives `abs`,
`min`, `max` and `clamp` one scheme each rather than one per numeric type, and `dot`, `vlength`,
`normalize` and `mix` one each rather than one per vector width.

[`TypePrinter`](languages.md#types-kt-typeprinter) renders a type two ways. `print` parenthesises every arrow, and is what diagnostics
and a box's inline result use; `printSignature` drops the parentheses that right associativity
makes redundant, and is what completion shows and what the cheatsheet's coverage guard compares
against. A printer names unification variables `'a`, `'b`, … in order of first appearance and
keeps those names for its own lifetime, so two types printed by one printer agree about which
variable is which, while two printers each start again at `'a`.

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">TypePrinter</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ml/type/Types/#L71)

Since `->` is right associative, a curried type only needs them when a function is an *argument*: `Float -> Float -> Vec2` rather than `(Float -> (Float -> Vec2))`, but still `(Int -> 'a) -> Int -> ['a]`. ## MorphoFLines.kt { #morphoflines-kt }

Drawing a MorphoHDL circuit with Field's FLines.

This is the half of the bridge morpho does not supply and Field does. Upstream renders with
SwissGL and a Canvas 2D fallback (`viewer.js`, `layout_renderer.js`, `bloom.js` — about 1,900
lines), none of which is vendored. Field already draws graphs, so a circuit becomes one FLine
per wire and one point-set per gate, and everything downstream — SVG export, the plane grid,
animation, the docs capture pipeline — comes along for free.

### Colour carries the simulation

By default wires are coloured by **signal arrival time**, which is what makes the picture worth
looking at rather than a hairball: the inputs are one end of the ramp, the critical path is the
other, and the difference between a ripple adder and a Brent–Kung is visible as a gradient
rather than inferable from a gate count.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/morpho/MorphoFLines.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/morpho/MorphoFLines/)

**Used in:** [Somebody else's language, running in Field](../morpho_examples.md)

## MorphoGenerator.kt { #morphogenerator-kt }

Where MorphoHDL programs come from when nobody writes them.

A sketch fixes everything about a cell that the search is *not* looking for — its name, its
ports, what it falls back into — and leaves the body open. That split is deliberate: "find a
circuit" with nothing fixed is a search over parse errors, and the interesting question is not
whether a random walk can discover the token `def`.

### Repair rather than reject

Mutation operators here are allowed to produce nonsense, and `MorphoProgramGenerator.repair`
projects it back into the region the width model calls plausible: an argument that names a wire
out of scope is rewired, a `SPLIT` of a one-bit bus is deleted, a recursive call that would not
narrow has its arguments resampled. Rejection-and-resample would be simpler and much worse —
with a rejection rate near one the search stops being a search.

The compiler still has the last word. Repair only makes candidates *likely* to compile; the
fraction that does not is reported as `MorphoSearchRun.failureRate` rather than hidden.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/morpho/MorphoGenerator.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/morpho/MorphoGenerator/)

## MorphoGenome.kt { #morphogenome-kt }

The thing a search actually mutates: a MorphoHDL **program, as text**.

That choice is the whole design. A generator could build netlists directly and skip the compiler,
and it would be faster and it would be a lie — the netlist would be Field's idea of what morpho
compiles a design into, and the resulting search would optimise against that idea rather than
against MorphoHDL. So a genome renders to source, upstream's `parse()` reads it, upstream's
`compileModule()` compiles it, and anything the search finds can be pasted into a morpho box and
will still be there tomorrow.

### The grammar this has to hit

`parser.js` is 190 lines and its accepted language is small (`parser.js:23-188`):

* top-level `Name = LUT(arity, value)`;
* `@morpho` or `@morpho(fallback=X)`, then `def name(a, b, c):`;
* SSA lines `t0, t1 = OP(x, y)`, one per line;
* `return x, y`.

That is all `MorphoGenome.render` emits, and it is why the rendered text is legible: it is not a
serialisation format, it is the language.

### Where the widths come from

MorphoHDL infers bus widths and never declares them, so a generator that ignores widths produces
mostly-invalid programs. [`MorphoWidthModel`](languages.md#morphogenome-kt-morphowidthmodel) is Field's *model* of that inference — it mirrors
`primitives.js`'s `SPLIT`/`CAT` and `compiler.js`'s `materializeLut` broadcast rule — and it is
used only to steer generation. The compiler remains the judge; the model's accuracy shows up as
`MorphoSearchRun.failureRate` and nowhere else.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/morpho/MorphoGenome.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/morpho/MorphoGenome/)

**Used in:** [Somebody else's language, running in Field](../morpho_examples.md)

## MorphoInterface.kt { #morphointerface-kt }

Field4 language adapter for MorphoHDL, a Python-syntax hardware-description language.

MorphoHDL programs describe recursive circuit structures that Field compiles via morpho's
own compiler on GraalJS and lays out with its Barnes–Hut kernel on GraalWasm. The result
lands on `Box.morphoCircuit`; a neighbouring Kotlin box reads it and draws with
`circuit.flines()`.

[`MorphoExecution`](languages.md#morphointerface-kt-morphoexecution) is the `BoxExecution` implementation. Setting a parent box's `isMorphoRoot`
to `true` turns its children into MorphoHDL boxes. Execute mode grows the circuit to
completion; launch mode expands a few cells per frame while relaxing the layout between
expansions, so the recursive division is visible in motion. `installMorpho` registers the
runtime; `installMorphoPlugin` starts the topology watcher.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/morpho/MorphoInterface.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/morpho/MorphoInterface/)

## MorphoSearch.kt { #morphosearch-kt }

Searching the space of MorphoHDL programs for one that computes something.

Three drivers, one evaluator, one generator. That is the arrangement the whole file exists for:
`MorphoSearch.random` is a **control arm** drawing from exactly the distribution
`MorphoSearch.hillClimb` and `MorphoSearch.evolve` mutate within, so a difference between their
results is a difference in *selection*. Reporting an evolutionary result without the control next
to it would say nothing at all — a generator good enough to make valid adders occasionally would
look like a successful search.

Every candidate is scored by compiling it with upstream's compiler and running the netlist that
comes out. See [`MorphoEvaluator`](languages.md#morphospec-kt-morphoevaluator).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/morpho/MorphoSearch.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/morpho/MorphoSearch/)

## MorphoSearchFLines.kt { #morphosearchflines-kt }

Drawing what a search did, as vector `FLine`s for `afield.stdlib.showPlaneGrid`.

Two figures, and between them they are the whole argument:

* `morphoConvergenceFLines` — best-so-far error against compiler invocations, one line per
  driver. This is where the **control arm** lives: the random-search line and the evolution line
  are drawn on the same axes at the same budget, so "the search found it" is a statement about
  the gap between two curves rather than about one number.
* `morphoParetoFLines` — gates against depth for every *correct* design found, with morpho's own
  hand-written designs marked. A search result that lands outside the human front is a result;
  one that lands on it is a different and much smaller result; and the picture says which.

Everything here is geometry. Nothing rasterises, so a figure scales, exports to SVG, and can be
redrawn every frame of a launched box while the search is still running.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/morpho/MorphoSearchFLines.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/morpho/MorphoSearchFLines/)

**Used in:** [Somebody else's language, running in Field](../morpho_examples.md)

## MorphoSpec.kt { #morphospec-kt }

What a MorphoHDL design is *supposed* to do, and how much it is allowed to cost — the half of a
search that morpho itself has no opinion about.

Everything in this file evaluates candidate designs by running them: [`MorphoRuntime`](languages.md#morphograal-kt-morphoruntime) compiles the
candidate's source with upstream's parser and upstream's compiler, [`MorphoSim`](languages.md#morphosim-kt-morphosim) runs the resulting
netlist, and [`MorphoTiming`](languages.md#morphosim-kt-morphotiming) — morpho's own `updateTimes()` — supplies the depth. Nothing here
models a circuit. A search whose fitness function was Field's idea of what a netlist would look
like would be searching Field's imagination, and the point of the bridge is that it does not have
to.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/morpho/MorphoSpec.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/morpho/MorphoSpec/)

**Used in:** [Somebody else's language, running in Field](../morpho_examples.md)

## NanoInterface.kt { #nanointerface-kt }

Field4 language adapter for the Nano 8-bit assembly language.

Nano is a compact virtual machine: 4 registers (r0–r3), 32 bytes of RAM with address
wrap, a small call stack, and an instruction set sized for emergence and artificial-life
grid experiments. [`NanoExecution`](languages.md#nanointerface-kt-nanoexecution) is the `BoxExecution` implementation; setting a parent
box's `isNanoRoot` to `true` turns its children into Nano assembly boxes.

`installNano` registers the runtime with Field's language dispatch; `installNanoPlugin`
starts the topology watcher that activates it when the box tree changes. `nanoAssemble`
and `Box.nanoDisassemble` are available to neighbouring Kotlin boxes that need to inspect
or construct the VM's byte representation directly.

## NanoVM.kt { #nanovm-kt }

Nano is a minimal 8-bit virtual machine designed for emergence and artificial-life simulations:
four registers, 32 bytes of RAM, and all but five of the 256 possible opcode bytes decoding to an
instruction.

The whole machine is:

 - `r0`–`r3`, 8-bit unsigned, so 0–255
 - 32 bytes of RAM, addressed modulo 32, so no address is out of range
 - flags `Z` (zero), `C` (carry), `S` (sign) and `O` (overflow)
 - a call stack eight deep, for `CALL` and `RET`
 - unsigned-byte arithmetic throughout, wrapping mod 256

Instructions are fetched from the program byte array passed to `NanoVM.run`, and `ram` is
separate data. `NanoVM.load` also mirrors the program's first 32 bytes into RAM, which is what
lets a program read its own text. `NanoInterface`'s launch mode calls `NanoVM.resetRegisters`
instead, leaving RAM alone so it carries state from one per-tick run to the next.

### Opcode map

[`Opcode`](languages.md#nanovm-kt-opcode) is the constant table, and `Opcode.twoReg` and `Opcode.oneReg` are the encoders.

| form | encoding | instructions | opcodes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| no operand | one byte | `NOP`, `HLT`, `RET` | `0x00`–`0x02` |
| one register | `base + reg`, 4 per op | `INC`, `DEC`, `NOT`, `NEG`, `CLR`, `OUT`, `RNG` | `0x04`–`0x1F` |
| two registers | `base + (dst shl 2) + src`, 16 per op | `MOV`, `ADD`, `SUB`, `MUL`, `AND`, `OR`, `XOR`, `CMP`, `LDR`, `STR` | `0x20`–`0xBF` |
| register and immediate or address | two bytes, 4 per op | `LDI`, `LDA`, `STA`, `ADDI`, `LDRR`, `STRR`, `SHL`, `SHR` | `0xC0`–`0xDF` |
| relative branch | two bytes, signed offset | `JMP`, `JZ`, `JNZ`, `JGT`, `JLT`, `JGE`, `JLE`, `JC`, `JNC`, `CALL` | `0xE0`–`0xE9` |
| absolute branch | two bytes, absolute address | `JMPA`, `CALLA` | `0xEA`–`0xEB` |
| two registers | `base + (dst shl 2) + src` | `DIV` | `0xEC`–`0xFB` |

Five bytes decode to nothing — `0x03`, and `0xFC`–`0xFF` past `DIV`'s last `(dst, src)` pair.
Each reports an unknown opcode and halts. That path matters here more than it would in a VM with
a fixed program: artificial-life work mutates programs, and `NanoAssembler`'s raw-byte directive
puts an arbitrary byte in front of the decoder too, so every one of the 256 has to either execute
or report. The GPU port in `nano_compute.glsl` decodes the same map.

### A program

```diffstatic {data-lang=nano}
; comment
start:
    ldi r0, 10     ; r0 = 10
    ldi r1, 0      ; r1 = 0
loop:
    add r1, r0     ; r1 += r0
    dec r0         ; r0--  (sets Z when r0 reaches 0)
    jnz loop       ; jump back if not zero
    out r1         ; print r1
    hlt
```

`NanoAssembler.kt` has the rest of the syntax, including the directive that places raw bytes in
the program stream and the fact that a label resolves to an offset for a relative branch and to
an address for `JMPA` and `CALLA`.

## PythonInterface.kt { #pythoninterface-kt }

Python as a Field main language: a box whose source is Python, executed **in this process** by
CPython through JEP.

In-process is the whole design and every consequence below follows from it. There is no
subprocess and no socket, so a Python box and a Kotlin box exchange objects rather than text; and
there is exactly **one interpreter and one namespace per Field process**, so two Python boxes
share globals whether or not you wanted them to. That is a deliberate trade — it is what makes a
cell in one box see a `DataFrame` another box built — and it is the first thing to know before
debugging "why does this variable already exist".

Read it in four layers:

 - **Configuration.** JEP needs a real CPython to bind against, chosen once and persisted:
   [`PythonSettingsRequest`](languages.md#pythoninterface-kt-pythonsettingsrequest), [`PythonSettingsStatus`](languages.md#pythoninterface-kt-pythonsettingsstatus) and [`PythonInstallResult`](languages.md#pythoninterface-kt-pythoninstallresult) are that
   negotiation, and `restartRequired` means it: a new interpreter binding cannot be swapped
   into a live JVM. `makeInterpreter` runs early and returns silently when nothing is
   configured, which is why a checkout with no Python simply has no Python boxes rather than a
   broken startup.
 - **[`PythonExecution`](languages.md#pythoninterface-kt-pythonexecution)**, the `BoxExecution`. Beyond the usual output proxying it carries the
   cooperative event loop: an `asyncio` loop implemented in Python that yields to Field's runloop
   instead of blocking it, so `await` inside a box does not stop the editor.
 - **Output.** Everything a box prints funnels through one formatter, and three cases are special
   on purpose: a `\r` becomes a Field progress bar (which is how `tqdm` renders as a real one),
   an object exposing `HTML`/`Image`/`Markdown`/`Math`/`JSON` renders as itself, and a library
   that tries to open a browser page — plotly's `fig.show()`, bokeh, folium — is intercepted and
   the HTML delivered into the box as an iframe `srcdoc`. Nothing here opens a browser.
 - **Registration.** `installPython` and `pythonTopologyNeedsUpdating` are the same two-call
   shape every main language uses; see `dev_docs/small_language_anatomy.md`.

A large part of this file is Python source held in Kotlin string literals — the event loop, the
display types, the output shims. It is code that has to run *inside* the interpreter, so it lives
here rather than in a `.py` on disk, where a fresh checkout could be missing it.

[Python in Field](../python.md) is the prose.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/python/PythonInterface.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/python/PythonInterface/)

## RectSL.kt { #rectsl-kt }

RectSL — Field's rectangle scene language, and the largest single file in the tree.

A RectSL program is a *finite animated scene made of rectangles*, written as a small stack
language inside a Kotlin triple-quoted string whose first line is `#rectsl`. It is not a
simulation and not a renderer: the language decides where rectangles are over a fixed duration
and what material metadata each one carries, and StackSL (`afield.stacksl`) decides how a
material shades. That division is the reason both are small.

### The pipeline, which is also the reading order

Four types, and every entry point in this file is a step between two of them:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
String  --tokenize-->  List<Token>  --eval-->  SceneProgram  --sample(t)-->  SampledScene  --lower-->  RectMesh
```

 - [`RectLangTokenizer`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-rectlangtokenizer) is the whole of the syntax. There is no parser: the language is
   postfix, so tokenizing *is* parsing.
 - [`RectLangVm`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-rectlangvm) is the evaluator, and where the vocabulary lives. Words spelled `->something`
   are mutators that write through to the active rect, group or scene; everything else
   transforms stack values. The arrow is part of the word.
 - [`SceneProgram`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-sceneprogram) is the compiled result and the value worth understanding first. It is
   **time-independent** — a wall, a duration, an fps and a list of nodes whose properties are
   [`Track`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-track)s rather than numbers — which is what makes a scene something you can ask questions
   of rather than only play. `sample(t)` walks it and returns a [`SampledScene`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-sampledscene), a flat
   z-ordered list of [`SampledRect`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-sampledrect)s with no tracks left in it.
 - `lowerSampledScene` turns that into a [`RectMesh`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-rectmesh): four [`RectVertex`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-rectvertex)es and six indices per
   rect, with colour, material index and per-object shader data interleaved, ready for an
   `afield.four` buffer.

[`RectAnimationOracle`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-rectanimationoracle) is the one object that names all five steps, and
`compileRectSL` is the same compile with host-built curves bound in by name — the
`afield.stdlib.Functions` half of the bridge, so a program can lay out an array from a curve the
host fitted or evolved.

### What the tracks buy, and why they are not just interpolation

Half this file is [`Track`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-track) and its implementations, because a property being a function of time
rather than a number is what the rest of the package is built on. A track is symbolic and
composable — [`TcbTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-tcbtrack) for Kochanek–Bartels keys, [`EasedScalarTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-easedscalartrack), [`TimeWarpTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-timewarptrack),
[`GateTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-gatetrack) for life windows, [`HeadingTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-headingtrack) for face-travel, plus unary/binary/ternary
combinators — so a scene can be *differentiated*, *fitted* (`RectSLFit.kt`), *measured*
(`RectSLCoverage.kt` computes exact pixel coverage in closed form) and *translated* to GLSL
(`RectSLGlsl.kt`) rather than only evaluated frame by frame.

### Where the rest of the package sits

`RectSLPattern.kt` / `RectSLPatternOps.kt` make a Tidal pattern the scene's structure — a
pattern is a track and an event is a live window. `RectSLSoftRaster.kt` is the differentiable
rasterizer, `RectSLFn.kt` lowers scenes into the `Functions` algebra, `RectSLSdfLook.kt` and
`RectSLGlsl.kt` are the two GPU paths, `RectSLSimplify.kt` shrinks a program, and
`RectSLEditorExtension.kt` is the three lines that register the browser-side editor mode.

[RectSL cheatsheet](../rectsl_cheatsheet.md) is the word-by-word reference with worked pictures;
[RectSL examples](../rectsl_examples.md) is the gallery.

**Used in:** [RectSL Inverse Animation](../rectsl_inverse_animation.md), [RectSL examples](../rectsl_examples.md), [RectSL cheatsheet](../rectsl_cheatsheet.md)

### GateTrack { #rectsl-kt-gatetrack }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">GateTrack</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">lo</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">NEGATIVE&#95;INFINITY</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">hi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">POSITIVE&#95;INFINITY</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Track</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/rectsl/RectSL/#L1059)

A hard visibility window — 1.0 while `lo <= t < hi`, else 0.0. Multiplied into an object's alpha, it makes the object pop into and out of existence at fixed times (bullet spawn/despawn). `lo`/`hi` default to ±infinity for one-sided gates.

### HeadingTrack { #rectsl-kt-headingtrack }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">HeadingTrack</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Track</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Track</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">eps</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span> <span class="p">/</span> <span class="mf">240.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">offset</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Track</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/rectsl/RectSL/#L1078)

Rotation derived from a pair of position tracks: the heading (direction of travel) of the point (x(t), y(t)). Because RectSL tracks are pure closed-form functions of time, the velocity is recovered by central finite difference — no simulation state — so a rect can auto-orient to its own trajectory. `offset` corrects for how the rect's art is drawn (0 = local +x points along travel).

## RectSLCoverage.kt { #rectslcoverage-kt }

The **exact** coverage a soft raster is approximating, and the measurement of how far off it is.

### Why the reference has to be exact

A soft rasterizer is only useful if you know what it is wrong about. The claim a differentiable
renderer makes is "coverage is a smooth function of the parameters"; the claim it must not make is
"coverage is *correct*". Between those two sits a bias, and a bias you have not measured is a bias
your fit has silently absorbed into its answer.

So this file computes the thing there is no argument about: the **area** of a pixel covered by the
scene, in closed form. A rect is a convex quadrilateral and a pixel is a convex box, so a single
rect's coverage is a convex-convex clip (`clipConvexToBox`, Sutherland–Hodgman) followed by the
shoelace formula (`polygonArea`) — exact in the arithmetic, with no sampling anywhere. A *union* of
rects is not convex, so that case goes to JTS, which is an external implementation of the same
quantity and therefore an oracle rather than a second opinion from the same author.
`RectSLSoftRasterTest` cross-checks the two on the single-rect case where both apply.

### The three biases, named

The measurement in `measureCoverageBias` is designed around the fact that there are three
*different* reasons soft coverage departs from area coverage, and lumping them together produces a
number that means nothing:

1. **Obliquity.** Every kernel in [`CoverageKernel`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt-coveragekernel) is a function of a single signed distance, so it
   is implicitly assuming the edge is axis-aligned. For an axis-aligned edge the exact area of a
   unit pixel on one side of it *is* `clamp(0.5 - d)`, so `CoverageKernel.LINEAR` at `beta` = one
   pixel has **zero** obliquity bias there — a fact worth checking, because if it does not come out
   at machine precision then either the kernel or the exact reference is wrong. As the edge rotates
   the true coverage curve becomes piecewise quadratic and the ramp cannot follow it.
2. **Feature scale.** A rect thinner than the band never lets coverage saturate. As
   width/`beta` → 0 the error tends to the whole of the feature's coverage, which is the regime
   where a soft raster is not an approximation of the picture at all.
3. **Union seams.** `min` of two signed distances is the union's distance *outside* the union and
   an under-estimate *inside* it, so where two rects abut the field reads about zero and coverage
   collapses towards 0.5 across a region that is entirely covered. This one is a property of the
   SDF, not of the kernel, and it is the reason [`CoverageComposite`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt-coveragecomposite) has two members.

Each is reported separately, over a population that is counted so that an empty population cannot
read as a pass: see `CoverageBiasRow.partialPixels` and `CoverageBiasRow.edgePixels`.

### Scope of the reference

Area coverage is defined for **opaque** geometry. A rect at alpha 0.4 has no area interpretation —
the exact answer to "what fraction of this pixel is covered" is still 1 if the rect fills it — so
`exactRaster` treats every visible rect as opaque and `measureCoverageBias` refuses a scene whose
rects are translucent rather than quietly comparing two different quantities.

## RectSLFit.kt { #rectslfit-kt }

Inverse animation: say where a rect should be and when, and solve for the numbers.

This is what the differentiable backend is *for*. A RectSL program is normally read forwards —
you write the tracks and the sampler tells you where the rects went. Once a track lowers to an
`Fn` the arrow turns round: [`FreeParamTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-freeparamtrack) marks the numbers you are willing to have chosen for
you, [`TrackFitTarget`](languages.md#rectslfit-kt-trackfittarget) says what the track should read at particular instants, and the exact
gradient of the lowered graph walks the parameters to the answer.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
# a bar whose height is unknown
1.0 free-param height
```
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val fit = track.fitParameters(listOf(TrackFitTarget(0.5, 3.0), TrackFitTarget(1.5, 0.0)))
fit.initialResidual   // where the seed was
fit.finalResidual     // where the fit ended
fit.fitted            // the same track, with the parameters substituted
```

### Why this is not simply `fitGradient`

`fitGradient` is the library's fitter and it does the right thing for a whole graph: it moves
**every** numeric leaf. A lowered track's leaves are mostly not parameters at all — they are the
key times, the clamp bounds, the `0.5` in an easing, the `-1.0` that mirrors a reversed clock.
Letting a descent move those would not fit a track, it would dismantle one. So the loss and the
Adam update here are the same shape as `fitGradient`'s, over a **mask**: only the θ slots that
`freeParameterSlots` identified as named parameters ever move — *slots*, plural, because a
lowering may use one sub-`Fn` more than once and each occurrence gets its own θ index. A heading
reads each of its position tracks twelve times. The slots of one name are one variable here:
gradients summed, one Adam moment, one step written to all of them.

Everything under the mask is borrowed rather than reimplemented. The gradient is
`Functions.Fn.gradientAt` — one forward interpretation and one backward sweep through the same
`FnFormulas` table `Fn.eval` is pinned against — and θ is read and written by
`extractParameters` / `applyParameters`, so index *i* means the same leaf here as it does there.

A track that does not lower cannot be fitted, and says so with the lowering's own reason rather
than a generic failure. A track that lowers but has no free parameters is refused too: descending
on an empty mask would report "converged" without having moved, which is the failure mode
`FnNonDifferentiable` exists to prevent.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/rectsl/RectSLFit.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/rectsl/RectSLFit/)

**Used in:** [RectSL Inverse Animation](../rectsl_inverse_animation.md)

## RectSLFn.kt { #rectslfn-kt }

RectSL tracks as differentiable `Fn` graphs — the third backend.

### Why there is a third backend at all

The track IR is symbolic rather than a closure, because a closure cannot be printed, compared,
serialized, rewritten, or emitted as GLSL. [`TrackOp1`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-trackop1), [`TrackOp2`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-trackop2), [`TrackOp3`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-trackop3) and [`TimeWarpKind`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-timewarpkind)
each carry an `eval:` and a `glsl:`; this file is the third column, `fn:`, and it is the one that
changes what RectSL can *do* rather than where it can run.

`afield.stdlib.Functions.Fn` is Field's own expression type, and `autodiff_fn.kt` differentiates
an `Fn` graph exactly with respect to its numeric leaves. So a track that lowers to an `Fn` is a
track you can take the derivative of, and therefore a track you can **solve**: declare where a
rect should be at some instant and let a gradient find the numbers that put it there. That is
`Track.fitParameters`, and it is the point of this file.

### The two identities that make it possible

`Fn` was not designed as a general expression language, and two gaps look fatal and are not.

**There is no "apply a unary function to another `Fn`'s value" op.** The differentiable value
transforms are `flip`, `abs`, `exp`, `log`, `pow`, `clamp`, `scaleY`, `offsetY` and pointwise
arithmetic — no `sin`. `Functions.sin` is an *oscillator* over the sample position,
`offset + amplitude·sin(2π·frequency·x + phase)`, which is not a composition. But its `phase`
child is evaluated **at x**, so

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
sin(frequency = 0, phase = u, amplitude = 1, offset = 0)   ==   sin(u(x))
```

exactly (`0 + 1·sin(2π·0·x + u)` collapses with no rounding). That single identity gives the
whole trigonometric family, which is most of the Penner easings.

**There is no piecewise-in-x op, and every keyframed track is piecewise.** A clamped-ramp sum
fixes it. For keys `(tᵢ, vᵢ)` and any segment shape `Sᵢ` with `Sᵢ(0) = vᵢ` and `Sᵢ(1) = vᵢ₊₁`,

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
v(t)  =  v₀ + Σᵢ [ Sᵢ(clamp01((t - tᵢ) / (tᵢ₊₁ - tᵢ))) - vᵢ ]
```

is *identically* the clamped piecewise interpolant: for t inside span j every earlier term is
`vᵢ₊₁ - vᵢ` and every later one is 0, so the sum telescopes to `vⱼ + (vⱼ₊₁ - vⱼ)·Sⱼ(u)`. Before
the first key everything is 0 and after the last everything is 1, which is exactly the sampler's
clamping. It needs only clamp / divide / multiply / add, all differentiable, and it is exact to
a few ulps rather than approximate. [`LinearScalarTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-linearscalartrack), [`EasedScalarTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-easedscalartrack) and [`TcbTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-tcbtrack)
(whose tangents `TcbTrack.hermiteSegments` has already resolved) all lower through it.

### Refusals are in the type

A wrong derivative is worse than no derivative, so the lowering never guesses. Every op declares
either a lowering or a refusal *with a reason* — [`RectSLFnLowering`](languages.md#rectslfn-kt-rectslfnlowering) — and `Track.toFn` propagates
the first refusal it meets. This is the same discipline `FnNonDifferentiable` already applies
inside the stdlib, and for the same reason: the gap has to be readable, or it grows in silence.

What is refused:

- `TrackOp2.MOD`. Kotlin's `%` on doubles is the *exact* remainder, and `a - b·trunc(a/b)` in
  double arithmetic is a different function once the quotient outgrows 53 bits: `1e17 % 3` is
  `1.0` and the reconstruction says `0.0`. Silently, and as a zero, which is indistinguishable
  from the guard having fired. A constant pair still folds.
- The pattern tracks ([`PatTrack`](languages.md#rectslpattern-kt-pattrack) and friends) — an interpreter over a mini-notation tree, not an
  expression of fixed shape. `PatPattern` is a `(PatArc) -> List<PatEvent>` lambda: there is
  nothing to inspect and no closed form to find, which is the same reason `FnNonDifferentiable`
  files `pat` itself, and makes this the one refusal here that cannot be closed. It has a name,
  `RECTSL_PATTERN_REFUSAL`, and a predicate that decides it from the track rather than from the
  sentence: `dependsOnPatternTrack`. It costs far less than four rhythm scenes in the gallery
  would suggest — 27 of 5020 tracks — because `pat` used as *scene structure* is unrolled at
  compile time into one gated rect per event, so no interpreter
  survives into the sampled IR, and `musicality-variation` lowers all 1096 of its tracks despite
  spending six `pat` verbs. What survives is a pattern still being asked a value of at sample
  time: a signal word read as a channel — `sine`, `cosine`, `saw`, `isaw`, `tri`, `square`,
  `perlin`, `rand` all push a `VSig`, and `VSig.asTrack` is a [`PatTrack`](languages.md#rectslpattern-kt-pattrack) — or one of the two
  gates the pattern layer installs on a rect's alpha, `->every` on the cycle count and
  `->degrade` on a per-event coin flip. Those are the same tracks the GLSL/SDF emitter has to
  bake rather than lower: the one place both backends meet the same wall.
- Degenerate keyed tracks: no keys at all (nothing to sample), or two keys sharing a time (a step
  between two named values, which the clamped-ramp identity cannot express).

Everything else lowers exactly, hard edges included. `Fn` has a first-class differentiable
`floor`, from which `ceil` is `-floor(-x)` and `fract` is `x - floor(x)`, both exact in IEEE, and
the `loop` and `pingpong` time warps follow for any window. `clamp01(floor(x) + 1)` is an *exact*
step — 1 at and above 0, 0 below, at every double including `-0.0` — which gives
[`HoldScalarTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-holdscalartrack) as `v₀ + Σ (vᵢ - vᵢ₋₁)·[t ≥ tᵢ]` and [`GateTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-gatetrack) straddling an edge as
`[t ≥ lo]·(1 - [t ≥ hi])`, the sampler's half-open boundary included. Zero-almost-everywhere is
the *truth* about a staircase rather than an approximation of one, so `Track.fitParameters`
refuses a parameter reachable only through a step instead of descending a gradient that cannot
move.

`withExactEndpoints` below covers the expo and elastic easings, whose closed forms do not reach
their own endpoints. `lowerHeading` covers [`HeadingTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-headingtrack) through `atan2`, and records the one
signed-zero corner where it parts
company with the sampler. `fnGuardedQuotient` guards the *divisor* of a near-zero division, as
`b·live + (1 - live)`, so nothing ever divides by a near-zero and no infinity is created to
mask; the sign of the suppressed zero is repaired by adding `fnZeroSelector`'s `-0.0`/`+0.0`,
since `x + -0.0` is the true additive identity on doubles and `x + +0.0` is not.

`dev_docs/stdlib_behaviour_changes.md` carries the dates on which each of those stopped being a
refusal, and what it means for a scene written before then.

### How the fidelity is checked

`RectSLFnBackendTest` is the reason to believe any of this. It reads
`src/jvmTest/resources/rectsl/track_characterization.txt` — every sampled rect of the gallery's
programs at 41 times, to full double precision — as data, and recomputes each rect's channels
through Fn-lowered tracks, so the oracle shares no code path with the thing under test. It
reports the worst disagreement, and it reports coverage, how much of the corpus lowered at all,
because a differential test that refused everything would otherwise read as a pass.

The corpus is not uniform in what it proves, and the difference is the reason to trust it. The
rows for the programs that predate this backend were dumped from code that knew nothing about
it, so a disagreement on one of those can only be this file's. The rows for the four
`musicality-*` programs were produced by the current `SceneProgram.sample`: still a real
differential, since the symbolic IR shares no code path with the sampler, but not independent of
a sampler bug introduced since. Nothing should be re-derived from those four as if it were.

## RectSLGlsl.kt { #rectslglsl-kt }

RectSL scenes as GLSL signed distance fields.

### Why this is a small file

RectSL looks like a big language to port, and almost none of it needs
porting. The stack VM is a *build-time* machine: `array`, `grid`, `radial`,
every selection word, `each`/`filter`, the chart and plotting layers, the
`{{ }}` Kotlin escapes — all of it runs once and is gone, leaving a
[`SceneProgram`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-sceneprogram): a flat list of nodes whose channels are [`Track`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-track)s. Only that
residue has to reach the GPU, and it is eleven track shapes and a 2D
transform.

### What the SDF is, and is not

This emits shape, not picture. A RectSL scene is painter's-algorithm 2D —
z-sorted rects composited with per-rect alpha, fill, and material. An SDF is
a set, and `min` is union, which has no notion of layering. So the emitted
`float` field answers "how far is this point from the nearest visible
rectangle" and drops fill, material, and layer order. What that
buys is everything a distance field is good at and a rasterized quad is not:
outlines and glows at any width, `smin` blending *between* rectangles,
boolean ops, per-pixel normals, and sub-frame motion blur — because time is a
uniform and every track is closed-form, so a fragment can sample the scene at
as many instants as it likes.

Visibility is not dropped. A rect whose alpha has been gated to zero by
`->appear` / `->vanish` / `->live` must not contribute a silhouette, so each
rect's alpha track is evaluated and tested before its distance is unioned in.

None of that list is aspirational, and it is more useful to say where the
evidence is than to restate the claim. [`RectSLSdfLook`](languages.md#rectslsdflook-kt-rectslsdflook) is that vocabulary as
data with one preset per capability, [`RectSLSdfShader`](languages.md#rectslsdflook-kt-rectslsdfshader) assembles a whole
fragment shader from it, and `RectSLGalleryHarness.renderSdf` renders each
preset — plus a side-by-side against the raster path — into
`public/docs/assets/rectsl/rectsl-sdf-*.png`. Two of them need the emitter's
cooperation rather than the look layer's, because they change the *set*: see
[`RectSLSdfOptions`](languages.md#rectslglsl-kt-rectslsdfoptions). To get it on screen and moving, replay
`dev_docs/agents/transcripts/rectsl_sdf_live.yaml`.

### Fidelity

Tracks are emitted symbolically, never sampled into tables: keyed tracks
become branch chains, TCB tracks become cubic Hermite spans with their
tangents precomputed on the CPU (`TcbTrack.hermiteSegments`), and the scalar
ops carry their own GLSL ([`TrackOp1`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-trackop1), [`TrackOp2`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-trackop2), [`TimeWarpKind`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-timewarpkind)). The
guards are reproduced rather than approximated — RectSL's divide-by-zero
returns 0, and its `mod` truncates where GLSL's floors.

The one unavoidable difference is precision: the CPU samples in `double` and
a shader runs in `float`. Expect agreement to about 1e-6 of a wall unit, not
to the ulp — which is now measured rather than assumed:
`RectSLGalleryHarness.measureSdfAgreement` reads the *compiled shader's* own
answers back out of a framebuffer and compares them against `SceneProgram.sample`
across eleven programs, and the worst disagreement is 2.5e-06 wall units.

What *is* approximated is now two tracks, not three. `->degrade`'s 64-bit
integer hash reads like something a shader cannot do and is not: it lowers
**exactly**, in `uvec2` lanes, with the threshold comparison done in integers so
no float enters the decision (see `emitDegradeGate` and `INT64_HELPER`). The two
that remain baked are the pattern queries, which are rational arithmetic over a
mini-notation tree — an interpreter, not a formula, and a different kind of
problem. There is nothing to lower symbolically even in principle: a
`PatPattern` is a `(PatArc) -> List<PatEvent>` lambda, so the emitter cannot tell
a `"bd*4"` from a `sine` from the outside, let alone find a closed form for it.
They go through `bakeTrack`, and what that costs depends on the track:

- a **rhythm** is piecewise constant, so the bake is exact except for where its
  edges are, and each edge is bisected to `BAKE_EDGE_TOLERANCE` — a microsecond,
  the same order as the millionth of a cycle [`PatTrack`](languages.md#rectslpattern-kt-pattrack) quantises its own queries
  to, which is the resolution the edge exists at in the first place;
- a **signal** — `sine`, `tri`, `perlin` — has no plateaus and no exactness to
  claim, so both a hold chain and a ramp through the samples are built and the one
  that measures closer wins. That is the ramp by 100x to 3000x, except on `saw`
  and `isaw`, whose once-a-cycle wrap a straight line would smear;
- `rand` is neither. It hashes the reduced rational instant it is handed, so it
  has no value *between* samples: a finer bake is a different signal, not a better
  approximation of this one. The emitter detects that by baking it twice — halving
  the rate leaves the error where it was — says so, and stops claiming otherwise.

Which of the three, and what it measured, is `RectSLSdfResult.bakes`; the same
thing as a sentence is `RectSLSdfResult.notes`. `RectSLSdfBakeTest` measures each
regime on the timeline, and `RectSLGlslSdfTest` holds the whole gallery to the
bound its own classification implies.

## RectSLPattern.kt { #rectslpattern-kt }

### RectSL's musical layer — the Tidal pattern language as scene structure

RectSL already had *time*: tracks, `->live birth life`, `->stagger-time`, `->split`. What it
did not have was **meter** — a shared clock, subdivision, and (the one that actually matters)
any way for repetition *n+1* to differ from repetition *n*. The array primitives distribute
copies in space and every copy plays the same clip. That is the difference between a loop and
a groove, and it is exactly the gap `afield.four.synth`'s pattern language fills.

The two languages turn out to be the same shape underneath, which is why this bridge is thin
rather than a translation layer:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
RectSL   interface Track<out T> { fun sample(t: Double): T }
Pattern  class PatPattern<A>    { fun events(arc: PatArc): List<PatEvent<A>> }
```

Both are **pure functions of time**, queryable out of order, with no simulation state —
`PatContractTest`'s purity and query-order properties assert it on one side, and RectSL's
closed-form tracks (the reason `HeadingTrack` can recover velocity by finite difference)
assert it on the other. So composing them needs no scheduler and no frame loop: a pattern
*is* a track ([`PatTrack`](languages.md#rectslpattern-kt-pattrack)), and an event *is* a life window (`patArray`).

#### What lives here

| § | words |
| --- | --- |
| clock | `->cps` `->tempo` `->beats-per-cycle` `->duration-cycles` `beats` `cycles` `cycle-secs` |
| pat | `pat` and its per-event context `t` `dur` `cyc` `step` `atom` `param` `param?` |
| patterns as values | `mini` `sine` `cosine` `saw` `isaw` `tri` `square` `rand` `perlin` `nums` `texts` `segment` `pat-range` `quantise` `bipolar` `euclid` `kolakoski` `kolakoski-gaps` |
| variation | `->every` `->off` `->jux` `->degrade` `->swing` `->press` `->iter` `->chunk` |
| layout | `strip` `->euclid` `->kolakoski` |
| out | `pat-events` |

#### Why a separate file

RectSL.kt is already 4.6k lines, and this layer is the only part of the language that depends
on `afield.four.synth`. Keeping the dependency in one file means the rest of RectSL still
compiles and reads without knowing the pattern language exists. The seams it needs from
RectSL.kt are deliberately small and marked `internal`: `RectLangVm.word`/`RectLangVm.mutator`
(so the musical words register through the same one path as every other word),
`RectLangVm.loopStack` and `LoopFrame.pat` (so `i`/`n`/`f` keep working inside a `pat` body),
`SceneBuilder.mapScalarTracks`, and `SceneBuilder.cps`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/rectsl/RectSLPattern.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/rectsl/RectSLPattern/)

## RectSLSdfLook.kt { #rectslsdflook-kt }

What to *do* with a RectSL distance field once you have one.

`RectSLGlsl.emitSdf` answers a single question per point — how far to the
nearest visible rectangle, at this instant — and its KDoc lists what that
buys: outlines and glows at any width, blending between rectangles, boolean
ops, per-pixel normals, sub-frame motion blur. Each of those is a handful of
GLSL lines over the same `float`, and writing them once per demo is how a
capability stays a claim. This file is the vocabulary instead: a look is data,
[`RectSLSdfShader`](languages.md#rectslsdflook-kt-rectslsdfshader) turns `(field, look)` into a complete fragment shader, and
`RectSLSdfLook.PRESETS` is one worked example of every advertised capability.

### What is a look and what is not

Two of the capabilities are *not* looks, and the split matters. Smooth-union
between rects changes the set itself, so it happens in the emitter
(`RectSLSdfOptions.blendRadius`) — a look can only carry the number and hand
it over. Boolean subtraction needs a *second* field, so a carving look is only
meaningful when the caller supplies one; `RectSLSdfShader.fragment` requires
it and says so.

### Why the edges are measured in pixels

Every softness here is expressed as a multiple of one screen pixel, recovered
per-fragment with `fwidth` on the world coordinate. That is the whole point of
a distance field over a rasterized quad: the same scene at 512px and at 4096px
has one-pixel edges at both, and no geometry was re-tessellated to get there.
Widths that describe the *scene* rather than the screen — an outline's
thickness, a contour's spacing, a bevel's depth — are in wall units, because
those are properties of the drawing and should zoom with it.
