## RectSLSimplify.kt { #rectslsimplify-kt }

An algebraic simplifier over the track IR — the last of the four capabilities `ddf732260` said a
symbolic IR would allow.

That commit's message named five things a closure cannot do: be printed, compared, serialized,
rewritten, or emitted as GLSL. GLSL shipped with it. `describe()` is the printing and
`substituteParameters` is a first, targeted rewrite. **Comparison came free** — the IR is data
classes, so two tracks built by the same `array` body are already `==`, which is exactly what the
GLSL emitter's function deduplication has been quietly relying on. This is the general rewriter,
and it is the one that needed comparison to exist: half the rules below fire on two subtrees being
structurally equal.

### What it is for

Not speed, primarily. RectSL's array words build per-copy channels by *offsetting* a constant, so a
hundred-copy array arrives at a backend as a hundred `BinaryDoubleTrack(const, const, ADD)` nodes,
and each backend has had to fold that itself: `trackConstantValue` exists because the GLSL emitter
needed it, and the `Fn` lowering calls the same function for the same reason. A fold is the
*smallest* rewrite, and having it live inside two emitters rather than over the IR is the tell that
the rewriter was missing.

The bigger reason is that a simplified tree is a smaller `Fn` graph, and an `Fn` graph's size is
the cost of both a sample and a gradient — `Fn.eval` walks every node, and `gradientAt` records
every node on a tape. A fit runs that thousands of times.

### The contract: every rule is bit-exact, and that is a real constraint

A simplified track must sample **bit-identically** to the original, not merely equal-to-tolerance,
which rules out several rewrites everyone writes by reflex. The gallery corpus caught the first
one: `0 - x` rewritten to `-x` disagrees at `x = 0`, because `0.0 - 0.0` is `+0.0` and `-(0.0)`
is `-0.0`.

A signed zero is not a curiosity in this IR. [`HeadingTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-headingtrack) takes `atan2` of a velocity, and
`atan2(+0.0, -1.0)` is `+pi` while `atan2(-0.0, -1.0)` is `-pi` — half a turn apart. A rewrite that
"only" changes the sign of a zero can therefore spin a rectangle through 180 degrees. So the rules
kept here are the ones exact for every double including both zeros, and the reflexive ones are
dropped with their reasons:

| rewrite | kept? | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| constant folding | yes | exact by construction — the folded value *is* what the chain evaluated to |
| `x - 0` -> `x` | yes | `x - (+0.0) == x` for every x, both zeros included |
| `x * 1`, `x / 1`, `x ^ 1` | yes | multiplicative identity preserves sign |
| `min(x, x)`, `max(x, x)` -> `x` | yes | structural equality; exact whatever x is |
| `-(-x)` -> `x`, `abs abs`, `saturate saturate` | yes | involution / idempotence, sign-exact |
| `clamp(x, v, v)` -> `v` | yes | `coerceIn(x, v, v)` is `v` |
| `shift 0`, `scale 1`, degenerate `loop`/`pingpong` | yes | the lookup is `t` unchanged |
| `x + 0` -> `x` | **no** | `(-0.0) + 0.0` is `+0.0`, so this flips a signed zero |
| `0 - x` -> `-x` | **no** | the rule the corpus caught, above |
| `mix(a, b, 1)` -> `b` | **no** | `a + (b - a)` is not `b` in floating point at all |
| `mix(a, b, 0)` -> `a`, `mix(a, a, t)` -> `a` | **no** | both end in `a + (+/-0.0)`, signed-zero unsafe |
| `x * 0` -> `0` | **no** | only valid for finite x, and nothing here proves x is finite |

Losing the additive identity costs less than it looks like it should: RectSL's array words build
per-copy channels by *offsetting a constant*, and the constant fold takes those whole.

Free parameters are never folded, for the same reason `trackConstantValue` takes a flag: a
[`FreeParamTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-freeparamtrack) holds a number but is not *a* number, and folding it away would delete the
thing a fit is meant to solve for.

### How it is checked

`RectSLSimplifyTest` runs it over the gallery and requires every rewritten channel to sample
**bit-identically** to the original at 41 times each, and to be a fixed point of a second pass.
The node-count reduction it prints is reported rather than asserted at any figure, because that
figure moves with the gallery and with the IR — a key value became a node when [`TcbKey`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-tcbkey) began
holding a track, for instance. Run the test to read the current one.

A plausible-looking rule that is wrong in one corner is this file's characteristic failure, and
bit-identity over the corpus already assembled for the differentiable backend is what catches it.

## RectSLSoftRaster.kt { #rectslsoftraster-kt }

The third lowering: a RectSL scene as a **differentiable raster**, so a picture can be fitted.

### Why this exists, and what it is not

`Track.fitParameters` turns the arrow round for one *track*: mark a number `free-param`, say what
the track should read at three instants, and the exact gradient of the lowered `Fn` walks the
number to the answer. What it cannot do is take a *target image*, because the derivative an image
fit needs is `d(pixel)/d(parameter)` and a per-track scalar lowering has no pixels in it. That was
recognised on 2026-08-06 and the image fit was abandoned rather than half-landed. This file is the
retry, on the terms the abandonment set: a soft rasterizer **whose coverage bias is measured**.
The exact reference that bias is measured against is `exactCoverage`; the numbers, and where they
say this is and is not usable, are in `dev_docs/RECTSL_SOFT_RASTER.md`.

### The one design decision worth arguing about

The obvious plan is "lower the scene to an `Fn`-valued signed distance field over (x, y, t)".
`Functions.Fn` cannot be that: it is a `(Double) -> Double`, one input and one output, and every
existing consumer of a lowered track — `freeParameterSlots`, `Track.substituteParameters`,
`Track.fitParameters` — reads its θ-vector as *the track's own leaves*. Smuggling x and y in as two
more θ leaves would make all of them quietly wrong about what they are solving for.

So the differentiable layer here is not `Fn`, it is [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) on an [`ADTape`](math.md#autodiff-kt-adtape) — which is what `Fn`'s own
gradient is built out of anyway. `FnAutoDiff.interpret` already re-reads an `Fn` graph in `AD`
arithmetic at an `AD`-tracked x, so:

- every **track** goes through the existing lowering, `Track.toFn`, unchanged;
- every track is then *interpreted* on the tape at the frame's time;
- the **geometry** — the ancestor-group composition, the rotate-into-local-frame, the exact box
  field, the `min` union — is written in `AD` directly, transcribed from the GLSL in
  `RectSLGlsl.PRELUDE` and the composition in `Transform2d.then`;
- the **coverage kernel** and the **image loss** go on the same tape.

One backward sweep then yields `d(loss)/dθ` for every parameter in the scene at once, with nothing
finite-differenced anywhere in the chain. That is strictly more than an `Fn` could have given.

### The scene-level θ ledger

`Track.fitParameters` masks θ within **one** `Fn`. A scene has eight tracks per rect and 183 rects
in the largest gallery scene, so it has hundreds of independent θ-vectors, and "index *i*" means
nothing until they are concatenated. [`SceneAdField`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt-sceneadfield) does that concatenation once: every channel
gets a contiguous block, `SceneAdField.theta` is the whole scene's leaves in block order, and
`SceneAdField.freeParameterSlots` re-maps each `free-param` **name** to its *global* slots —
unioned across channels, because one name legitimately reaches several of them. The
gradient-summed, step-applied-to-every-slot discipline of `Track.fitParameters` carries over
unchanged; only the index space is new.

### Cost, and why a frame is a separate object

[`ADTape`](math.md#autodiff-kt-adtape) records five parallel arrays per operation and never shrinks. A 128² raster over a
30-rect scene, naively taped, is ~14M nodes — half a gigabyte. But a shape's *transform* depends
only on (θ, t) and not on the pixel, so `SceneAdField.frameAt` evaluates all of it once and
[`SceneAdFrame`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt-sceneadframe) hands back only what varies per pixel: centre, rotation, half-extent, alpha. The
per-pixel cost drops to about twenty tape nodes per rect, and because an image loss is a *sum*
over pixels its gradient is additive — so `softRasterLossAndGradient` walks the image in row
chunks, one tape per chunk, and accumulates. Memory becomes a choice rather than a limit.

### Fidelity, and the honesty check that is not optional

A second interpreter of the same graph is exactly the situation where a *slightly different
function* gets differentiated confidently. `autodiff_fn.kt` has a name for the guard against that
— `FnAutoDiff.worstValueDisagreement` — and `toAdField` runs it on every channel it lowers,
recording the worst in `SceneAdField.worstChannelDisagreement`. A channel whose `AD` reading parts
company with its own `Fn.eval` is refused, not averaged in.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/rectsl/RectSLSoftRaster.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/rectsl/RectSLSoftRaster/)

## Asta.kt { #asta-kt }

Source-to-source rewriting of a JavaScript box, over Nashorn's parse tree.

JavaScript has no operator overloading, so in a RemoteJS box `a + b` on two vectors concatenates
their string forms and `a - b` is `NaN`. This pass rewrites the source before it ships: each
binary `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `^` becomes a call to a global named for the operator, so `a + b`
leaves here as `__PLUS__(a,b)`. The head supplies those globals in `field/asta.js`, where
`__PLUS__`, `__MINUS__`, `__MULTIPLY__` and `__DIVIDE__` work componentwise on `THREE` vectors,
promote an array of two or three numbers to a vector first, let an operand join the protocol by
defining its own `__PLUS__` (or `__RPLUS__`, for the right-hand side), and throw a named error
where plain JavaScript would hand back `NaN` or `"[object Object]"`. `XOR` is in the trap set
here and has no counterpart there.

`executeRemoteJS` runs the pass when its `doASTA` flag is set, which is the default. The
Kotlin/JS path sets it false, because Kotlin has `operator fun plus` of its own and a compiled
box needs no rewriting.

The pass also recovers a source location. Nashorn parses at ES6 while the browser is the
authority on whether newer syntax is valid, so a diagnostic raised here is held rather than
shown, and used only to fill in the line and column of a `SyntaxError` that the head reported
without one; an error the head raises at run time keeps its own location. A parser
`AssertionError` is caught, notified, and the source returned unrewritten, so a construct
Nashorn cannot read costs the operators rather than the run.

Rewriting is textual, so offsets do the work, and Nashorn's need correcting before they can
index the string. A string literal's quotes fall outside its reported extent, and a node that
reports a narrower span than its own children is widened to cover them. Replacements run
back-to-front so an earlier edit cannot move a later one, and the header of a `for` loop is
excluded from rewriting entirely, because an edit inside it shifts the offsets of everything the
loop spans. Field's `//# sourceURL=` trailer is split off before parsing and appended again
afterwards.

`Options` gates the whole pass. `overloads` is on, and is the operator rewrite above; `numbers`
is off, and rewrites each numeric literal to `__NUMBER_LITERAL__(start, end, text)`, for which
this tree carries no head-side definition; `functionRewrite` is off and has no effect beyond
making the pass run at all. With all three off, `parseAndReconstruct` returns its input
unchanged.

## KotlinJs.kt { #kotlinjs-kt }

SPIKE — a "Kotlin in the head" main language. A box flagged `mainLanguage = "kotlinjs"` (or its
legacy `isKotlinJsRoot` root flag) compiles its Kotlin source to JavaScript via
[`KotlinToJsCompiler`](languages.md#kotlintojscompiler-kt-kotlintojscompiler) (PLAIN_DCE: self-contained, tree-shaken, eval-able) and ships it to the
connected browser / visionOS head over the same WebSocket transport RemoteJS uses.

This reuses RemoteJS's transport wholesale (`compileAndSendKotlin` → `executeRemoteJS` with
`doASTA = false`); it only swaps *what runs the box* (Kotlin→JS compile) for the JS path. Kotlin
gets native operator overloading (no ASTA), real types, and compile-time diagnostics at the
source line. See dev_docs/kotlin_to_js_spike.md.

## KotlinJsHeadProfiles.kt { #kotlinjsheadprofiles-kt }

Which remote head a Kotlin/JS box runs on, chosen by a marker on its first line.

A box whose main language is `kotlinjs` compiles to JavaScript and ships to a head over the
RemoteJS transport, but the heads are not interchangeable: each has a different set of globals
loaded, and Kotlin can only be typed against the globals its target actually has. A profile is
that pairing. It carries the `external` declarations spliced in front of the author's source
before compiling, a second surface used for completion, and the transport and lifecycle calls
that put the compiled JavaScript in front of a head.

`KotlinJsHeadProfiles.resolve` reads a `// {{ name }}` marker on the first non-blank line and
returns a [`KotlinJsHeadSelection`](languages.md#kotlinjsheadprofiles-kt-kotlinjsheadselection). A name is matched case-insensitively against an id or an
alias:

 - `remote` — the plain RemoteJS head; aliases `default` and `remotejs`, and what a box with no
   marker at all gets.
 - `remoteAR` — the A-Frame and THREE scene head; aliases `ar`, `remote-ar`, `remotear`.
 - `tone` — the Tone.js computer-music head; aliases `tonejs` and `music`.
 - `visionmetal` — the visionOS Metal head; aliases `metal` and `vision-metal`.

An unknown name raises instead of falling back, because a box compiled against the wrong globals
type-checks and then fails in the head. The same reasoning gates delivery at run time: a head
has to report the capability keys its profile requires in its `initialize` payload before it is
counted or sent to, so `// {{ tone }}` reaches a head with Tone loaded and no other.

Two further things `resolve` does, both about line numbers. It blanks the marker's line rather
than removing it, so the lines the compiler reports still line up with what the author sees. And
`resolveForBox` re-reads the marker from the box's stored `code` when the source handed to it
carries none, which is what fragment and symbol execution pass when only a selection is being
run.

The two implementations behind the sealed class mean different things by sending. The WebSocket
one hands its JavaScript to `executeRemoteJS` with `doASTA = false`, broadcasts to every
connected head that matches, and reports results back through the box's output. The visionOS one
publishes a Metal program on the box instead and reports success without waiting, because that
publication is durable and replays for a native head that subscribes later. Its `uniforms`
option is the only marker option here: slot order is what the head turns into `#define u_NAME`,
so it is declared rather than inferred, and the inference that covers an absent declaration says
what it guessed.

## KotlinToJsCompiler.kt { #kotlintojscompiler-kt }

SPIKE — Kotlin source -> JavaScript, for RemoteJS boxes.

This mirrors what JetBrains' `kotlin-compiler-server` (KotlinToJSTranslator) does: a two-phase
K2 compile of a self-contained Kotlin snippet into a single, eval-able JS module that the existing
RemoteJS transport ships to the browser / visionOS "graphics head" over the WebSocket bus.

    phase 1:  source.kt      --( -Xir-produce-klib-file )-->                 <module>.klib
    phase 2:  <module>.klib  --( -Xir-produce-js, -Xinclude, -Xir-dce )-->   <module>.js

What this buys a box author is Kotlin: real types, completion, and native `operator fun plus`
vector and matrix math, so a Kotlin box needs none of the operator rewriting `Asta.kt` does for a
JavaScript one. The result runs unchanged in the head via `executeRemoteJS` with
`doASTA = false`.

Output is a `plain` module that self-invokes `main`, so the head's `global.eval(code)` runs it
with no changes. Dead-code elimination is what keeps that module small enough to ship on every
compile: it tree-shakes the stdlib, taking a trivial program well under the ~600 KB an
unshaken one contributes, and `KotlinToJsSpikeTest` holds the emitted JS under 50 000
characters.

Two execution modes (`Mode`):
 - IN_PROCESS: calls `K2JSCompiler().exec(...)` directly, with no JVM launch to pay for. The K2
   REPL (`KotlinInterface2`) already holds a live IntelliJ application environment in this JVM
   and `K2JSCompiler` reuses the process-wide `getOrCreateApplicationEnvironment`; the two
   coexist, and a throw from that call falls back to SUBPROCESS rather than failing the compile.
 - SUBPROCESS: spawns `java -cp <this app's classpath> K2JSCompiler`. Fully isolated, and reuses
   the embeddable compiler already on the runtime classpath. Slower, by a cold JVM per compile.

Follow-up (see dev_docs/kotlin_to_js_spike.md): incremental compiles via JsIrCompilerWithIC, and a
typed `external` façade over the head runtime (THREE / A-Frame / Field JS).

## RemoteJS.kt { #remotejs-kt }

RemoteJS — JavaScript that runs in a *browser somewhere else*, written in a Field box here.

The value proposition is not "Field can run JavaScript". It is that the box is on this machine and
the execution is on a **head**: a browser tab, an Electron window, a phone, a Vision Pro. A head
connects inbound over the WebSocket Field already has, announces an id and its capabilities, and
from then on a box can be pointed at one head, at all of them, or at a filtered subset.
`knownOpenRemoteClients` and `remoteClientCapabilities` are that registry, keyed by head id, and
they are the reason nearly everything here takes a `filterSession` rather than a connection.

### The one function to read

`executeRemoteJS` is the language. Its parameter list *is* the semantics, and three of them carry
most of the weight:

 - `doASTA` routes the source through [`Asta`](languages.md#asta-kt-asta) first, which rewrites each binary operator into a
   call the head's `asta.js` defines, so vector arithmetic in a box means what it looks like.
   That pass also parses, and its diagnostics fill in the line and column of a `SyntaxError` the
   browser reported without one; an error raised at run time keeps its own location. Turn it
   off, as the Kotlin/JS path does, and a box gets neither.
 - `lifecycleName` and `launchable` are what make a fragment restartable and time-scrubbable
   rather than fire-and-forget, and `timeStart`/`timeEnd` are the window it is live for.
 - `handleTo` is the return channel: a head can send values back, dispatched through
   `returnHandlers`, so this is a duplex language and not a one-way pipe.

[`RemoteJSExectution`](languages.md#remotejs-kt-remotejsexectution) is the `BoxExecution` for a box written *in* JavaScript;
`installRemoteJSMainLanguage` registers it, and `becomeRemote` is the imperative version for a
box that is being converted. Note the two ids: this file registers `remotejs`, and `KotlinJs.kt`
beside it registers `kotlinjs` — the same transport, but the box is written in Kotlin and
cross-compiled, with `KotlinToJsCompiler.kt` doing the compiling and
[`afield.remotejs.KotlinJsHeadProfile`](languages.md#kotlinjsheadprofiles-kt-kotlinjsheadprofile) describing what each kind of head can be asked to do. Two
main languages, one package.

`dev_docs/small_language_anatomy.md` is the map of the integration points every main language
touches.

## StackSL.kt { #stacksl-kt }

StackSL — a concatenative shading language that compiles to GLSL, in one file with no runtime.

A StackSL program is a sequence of words over a `vec4` stack, and it lowers to exactly one GLSL
function: `vec4 stack(vec4 stack_in)`, conventionally called with `vec4(x, y, z_or_hash, time)`.
There is no interpreter here and nothing executes on the JVM — `StackSLCompiler.compile` is a
source-to-source translation, which is why the whole language is a compiler and a diagnostic
type and nothing else.

### The three values to know

 - [`StackSLCompileOptions`](languages.md#stacksl-kt-stackslcompileoptions) decides the shape of the emitted GLSL rather than the meaning of the
   program: the symbol prefix, the entry point name, whether a header and samplers are declared,
   which textures `sample` may read, and — the one that changes semantics —
   `defaultValues`, the wrap/default convention used when a word wants an operand the stack does
   not have. `tolerant` decides whether that is a warning or an error.
 - [`StackSLCompileResult`](languages.md#stacksl-kt-stackslcompileresult) is GLSL, diagnostics and an analysis. `ok` is *diagnostics with no
   ERROR*, not "the GLSL is non-empty", because a tolerant compile emits usable GLSL and
   complains at the same time.
 - [`StackSLAnalysis`](languages.md#stacksl-kt-stackslanalysis) is the part worth reading before debugging a program that produced a black
   frame. Per function it reports `maxStackDepth`, `finalStackDepth`, `producedValues`,
   `usedValues` and `prunedValues`, plus [`StackSLDanglingWire`](languages.md#stacksl-kt-stacksldanglingwire) for each value that was pushed and
   never consumed. A definition whose arity does not work out is **pruned silently** in the
   emitted shader — the diagnostic and this analysis are the only places it says so.

`compileStackSL` and `compileStackSLToGlsl` are the two convenience entry points; the second
throws away everything except the source, which is usually the wrong trade.

### Where StackSL sits relative to its neighbours

`afield.stdlib/stacksl.kt` — on the [Graphics](graphics.md) page, because it is host API rather
than language — is how a box actually reaches a StackSL string. `afield.rectsl` compiles through
this file: RectSL decides where rectangles are, StackSL decides how their materials shade, and
`RectSLGlsl.kt` is the join. `VolumetricNoise.kt` beside this file is the noise vocabulary the
emitted GLSL calls into.

[StackSL cheatsheet](../stacksl_cheatsheet.md) is the word-by-word reference;
[StackSL examples](../stacksl_examples.md) is the gallery.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stacksl/StackSL.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stacksl/StackSL/)

**Used in:** [StackSL examples](../stacksl_examples.md)

## VolumetricNoise.kt { #volumetricnoise-kt }

StackSL's volumetric noise family: `noise3`, `fbm3`, `fbmd3`, `warp3`, `curl3`, `worley3`,
`noise4`, `fbm4` — eight words that work as true 3D and 4D fields.

### Why a separate family

StackSL's original `noise` and `fbm` are two-dimensional. The word lowers to
`_noise(input.xy + input.zw * 0.07)`, so a vec4 carrying a position and a time is squashed
into a plane: z enters at one fourteenth the weight of x, as a shear rather than as a third
dimension. On a volume seen down z that reads as one fixed pattern imprinted at every depth.
The two-slice-sum workaround (`f(x,y) + f(y,z) + f(z,x)`) is what people write instead, and
it costs three fbms and does not give a 3D field — it gives three sheared 2D ones.

### Three properties the 2D words lack

**The range really is [0,1).** `_fbm(vec2)` sums five octaves at amplitudes 0.5 0.25 0.125
0.0625 0.03125, which total 0.96875, not 1 — so the usual `0.5 -` recentering leaves a
constant bias of about -0.031. A constant force integrates into a drift instead of averaging
out. Here the amplitude sum is accumulated at runtime and divided out, so the range is exactly
[0,1) for any octave count, lacunarity and gain.

**The hashes contain no `sin()`.** `_hash11(float)` uses `fract(sin(p * 127.1) * 43758.5453123)`,
and `sin` is not bit-portable: its precision is implementation-defined, it loses all meaning
for large arguments, and no CPU implementation can be trusted to agree with a GPU's.
`_hash21(vec2)` — the hash that actually feeds `_noise` and `_fbm` — has no `sin` at all; it
is `fract(p * vec2(123.34, 456.21))`, `p += dot(p, p + 45.32)`, `fract(p.x * p.y)`, so it is
already multiply/add/fract and already IEEE-754 exact. (Exact is not the same as stable:
`fract` of a large product amplifies a last-bit difference in its argument to O(1), which is
why an exactly-specified noise can still disagree visibly across backends.) The reason this
family could not use `_hash21` is dimensionality: `_hash21` takes a `vec2`, and a 3D/4D family
needs a hash over 3 and 4 inputs. The hashes below are multiply/add/fract only, which makes
[`VolumetricNoiseReference`](languages.md#volumetricnoise-kt-volumetricnoisereference) a real reference rather than an approximation.
`StackSLCpuVolumetricCrossCheckTest` evaluates the emitted GLSL against every function here,
bit-for-bit.

**`curl3` is divergence-free by construction.** It is the curl of a vector potential taken
with central differences at one shared epsilon. Discrete shift operators commute, so the
discrete divergence of the discrete curl cancels term for term and is zero up to float rounding
— see `VolumetricNoiseTest`. Particles advected through it swirl instead of piling into sinks.

### Constants

[`VolumetricNoiseConstants`](languages.md#volumetricnoise-kt-volumetricnoiseconstants) is the single source of truth for the family's shared constants —
the octave defaults, lacunarity, gain, the finite-difference epsilons, the hash multipliers and
the per-octave rotation. The Kotlin reference reads them and the emitted GLSL interpolates
them, so the two cannot drift apart. `VolumetricNoiseTest`'s `every shared constant appears in
the emitted GLSL` fails if one is ever typed into the shader text by hand. The algebraic
coefficients inside [`VolumetricNoiseReference`](languages.md#volumetricnoise-kt-volumetricnoisereference) — the `mix` weights, the smoothstep polynomial —
are spelled out at their call sites instead, because they are the definition of the operation
rather than a tunable value.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stacksl/VolumetricNoise.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stacksl/VolumetricNoise/)

### VolumetricNoiseReference { #volumetricnoise-kt-volumetricnoisereference }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">VolumetricNoiseReference</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stacksl/VolumetricNoise/#L177)

The CPU twin of the GLSL emitted by `volumetricNoiseHelperSource`. Every function here is a statement-for-statement transliteration of its shader counterpart, in `Float`, using only operations GLSL and the JVM both round identically. It exists so the family's semantics — ranges, continuity, `worley3`'s F1 <= F2, `curl3`'s divergence — can be asserted without a device, which is the only kind of test StackSL has ever been able to have.

## GlslInterpreter.kt { #glslinterpreter-kt }

The evaluator for parsed GLSL shaders, tree-walking and single-threaded per invocation.

It holds no state between invocations except the globals the caller supplies, so a raster can
be rendered by running one [`GlslInvocation`](languages.md#glslinterpreter-kt-glslinvocation) per row across as many threads as there are cores
— see [`StackSLCpu`](languages.md#stackslcpu-kt-stackslcpu).

### Two design choices

**Control flow as a return value, not an exception.** Each statement reports what it did to
control flow — normal, break, continue, return or discard — as an ordinary return value, and
the caller unwinds. The tree-walking pattern normally uses a control-flow exception, but the
volumes here are large: `_fbm` returns from inside a five-iteration loop, and a 512×512 render
evaluates that `return` 1.3 million times per program, which is too many to assume a
stack-trace-bearing exception is free.

**One flat frame per function call, with block scopes as marks into it.** Entering a block
records the current top of the frame and leaving truncates back to it, giving correct GLSL
shadowing with no per-block allocation. Lookup is a backwards linear scan, which for the
emitted subset (never more than about a dozen live names) beats a hash map.

## GlslParser.kt { #glslparser-kt }

A parser for the GLSL that StackSL's emitter actually produces.

### Why a parser and not a second backend in the compiler

`StackSLCompiler` has no symbolic node to hang a CPU arm off: its one internal node is
`StackValue(id, expression: String, …)` and `expression` is already GLSL text, built by
`String`-returning lambdas in `StackSL.kt`. Adding an `eval:` beside every `glsl:` — the
RectSL `TrackOp` shape — would mean rewriting the emitter word by word, and every one of
those rewrites is a chance to make the CPU arm disagree with the GPU arm. That disagreement
is the exact defect this backend exists to rule out: a hand-written CPU twin that diverged
from its own emitter.

Parsing the emitter's output means the CPU backend consumes *the same text the GPU consumes*,
byte for byte, and cannot drift from the shipping emitter by construction. It also needs zero
edits to `StackSL.kt`, so it cannot regress the GPU path at all.

### What the subset is, measured

Dumped for all 31 committed gallery programs (1472 lines of emitted GLSL), the entire surface
is: scalar/vector/matrix declarations, `=`/`+=`/`-=`/`*=`/`/=`, `if`, `for (int i = …; …; i++)`,
`return`, function definitions, and about 30 builtins. **No ternary, no `while`, no `switch`,
no structs, no arrays, no bit operators.** This parser covers a little more than that (ternary,
`while`, `do`, `break`/`continue`, interface blocks) so the first shader that reaches slightly
further does not fail; anything genuinely outside throws [`GlslUnsupported`](languages.md#glslvalue-kt-glslunsupported) with the token
quoted rather than guessing.

## GlslValue.kt { #glslvalue-kt }

The value model for the GLSL-subset interpreter behind StackSL's CPU backend.

### Why Float, not Double

The thing being mirrored is a GPU fragment shader whose `float` is IEEE-754 binary32. Every
intermediate here is therefore a `Float`, and every builtin rounds to `Float` at every step,
including the ones Kotlin would rather do in `Double` (`kotlin.math.sin` takes and returns
`Double`, so those are computed wide and narrowed once — see `f1`). Widening an intermediate
would make the CPU result *more* accurate than the shader and therefore a worse reference:
the goal is to reproduce the shader, not to improve on it.

Two consequences bound what any CPU implementation can agree with a GPU on, and neither is a
defect in this file:

  - `sin`, `cos`, `exp`, `log`, `pow`, `atan` are IMPLEMENTATION-DEFINED in GLSL. The spec
    gives them no accuracy requirement at all beyond monotonicity in places. So no CPU
    implementation can be bit-exact with a GPU's, even in principle, and any program that
    reaches one of them can only be compared under a tolerance.
  - Even the exact operations do not compose exactly, because a GPU may CONTRACT `a * b + c`
    into a fused multiply-add with one rounding while the JVM performs two. Kotlin has no
    `fma`-free guarantee to offer here either way; what it does have is no automatic
    contraction, so this interpreter is the *unfused* reading of the shader.

The interesting failure is neither of those. `fract` of a large product amplifies a last-bit
difference in its argument to O(1) — so `_hash21`, which is multiply/add/fract only and
therefore exact operation by operation, can still produce a visibly different image from a
backend that differed by one ulp three operations earlier. That is chaos, not error, and the
gallery characterisation reports it separately from tolerance.

## StackSLCpu.kt { #stackslcpu-kt }

StackSL's CPU backend: the same GLSL a GPU would run, evaluated one pixel at a time on the JVM,
so a StackSL program can be rendered, unit-tested, diffed and documented with no graphics context
at all.

[`StackSLCpu`](languages.md#stackslcpu-kt-stackslcpu) is the entry point and [`CpuRaster`](languages.md#stackslcpu-kt-cpuraster) is what comes back: RGBA floats with row 0 at the
top, quantised the way a `VK_FORMAT_R8G8B8A8_UNORM` attachment does, and encodable straight to
PNG. `StackSLCpu.renderStill` is the one-liner a box wants.

What the backend is exact about is the *program*. `StackSLCpu.renderFragment` takes a complete
fragment shader as text and knows nothing about StackSL; the StackSL half compiles a program with
`StackSLCompiler` and substitutes the result into a `{{ stack.auto.<slot> }}` template, which is
the same tag the production expansion path in `afield.stdlib.shaders` fills. Both paths therefore
receive the same string, and nothing about a word's behaviour is restated here: change what the
emitter makes of `fbm` and this backend changes with it on the next call, with no edit. Tests pin
the two copies that make that true: `StackSLCpuExpansionTest` compares the compile options against
the production path's, and `StackSLCpuStillTemplateTest` compares the gallery's fragment template
against the committed one in the gallery workspace.

It is a reference, not a renderer. It is an interpreter, so it is orders of magnitude short of a
GPU, and `StackSLCpu.renderStill` states a cost for one program at one size. It is not bit-exact
either: GLSL leaves `sin`, `cos`, `exp`, `log`, `pow` and `atan` implementation-defined, so a
program that reaches one of them can only be compared under a tolerance. [`GlslValue`](languages.md#glslvalue-kt-glslvalue) has that
argument in full, including the case where operations that *are* exact still diverge visibly.
